posts.title: The cookie banner your analytics doesn't need
posts.body:
Quick question for anyone running a website: why is your cookie banner there?

For many sites, the honest answer is analytics. The tracking script sets cookies and collects personal data, so visitors get a pop-up before they've read a single word.

Plausible works differently. It doesn't use cookies and doesn't collect personal data. That means Plausible itself doesn't need a cookie banner or a GDPR consent form.

You still see what matters: where visitors come from, which pages they read, and what they do. It's all on one clear dashboard.

If analytics is the only reason your banner exists, it might be time to rethink it. Start a free trial at https://plausible.io

posts.title: Why being self-funded matters for an analytics tool
posts.body:
We're self-funded. No outside investors.

People sometimes ask why that should matter to someone choosing a web analytics tool. Here's the plain answer.

When a company raises venture money, a clock starts. Growth has to keep pace with the next round. That pressure tends to leak into the product: collect a bit more data, push a few more upsells, and consider a data deal that looks tempting in a bad quarter.

We don't have that clock.

Plausible is independent, self-funded and profitable. We're based in the EU. We don't sell customer data, and our business doesn't depend on it.

We're paid by our subscribers, over 21,000 of them. Not by selling what we learn about their visitors. That keeps our incentives simple: build analytics that site owners want to keep paying for.

If you're deciding where your website's traffic data should live, ask every vendor one question:

How do you make money?

The answer tells you most of what you need to know about what happens to your data.

posts.title: Every analytics tool is paid for by someone: the pricing-page test
posts.body:
Every analytics tool on your site is paid for by someone. Before you install one, it's worth knowing who.

An analytics script runs on every page you publish and sees every visit. When the tool costs you nothing, the bill still gets paid somewhere: by investors expecting a return, by an ad business, or by the data itself. None of that is automatically bad, but whoever pays decides what the tool is built to do with your visitors' visits.

So the honest check takes five minutes. Open the vendor's pricing page and its privacy policy side by side, then answer two questions. Who pays for this? And is my visitors' data part of what they get?

Here is our answer at Plausible. More than 21,000 site owners pay for it. We're self-funded, profitable and based in the EU, and we don't sell customer data. The script uses no cookies and collects no personal data, so there is no personal information about your visitors on our side for anyone to buy.

It also means Plausible isn't free. I'd rather you knew exactly what you're paying and who you're paying than wonder later.

What made you take a harder look at a free tool you'd relied on for years?

posts.title: Your cookie banner is a symptom: a short audit
posts.body:
Someone clicks through to your site from a newsletter. Before they read your headline, a box asks them to accept cookies and covers part of the page they came to see.

That box exists because something on your site sets cookies or collects personal data. On many sites the list starts with analytics, then grows with chat widgets, ad pixels and embedded videos. So the banner gets longer every time someone adds a tool, and nobody goes back to check what each one is asking permission for.

Which means the fix starts with an audit, not a nicer banner design. List every cookie your site sets, note which script set it, and decide whether that script still earns its place in front of your visitors.

Analytics is one item you can take off that list. Plausible uses no cookies and collects no personal data, so it doesn't need a cookie banner or a GDPR consent form. Your other scripts still need checking, and the document below shows how to do it in your browser.

posts.title: The analytics script you load on every pageview
posts.body:
Your analytics script loads on every page, for every visitor, for as long as it's installed. Most site owners have never checked how big it is.

That makes its size a recurring cost rather than a one-off. Each visitor downloads it alongside the content they came for, and on a slow mobile connection it competes with your own pages for the same bandwidth.

You can check yours in a couple of minutes. Open your homepage in Chrome, press F12, open the Network tab, filter by JS and reload. Sort by size and find your analytics script. If it sits near the top of that list, it's one of the heaviest things your visitors download on every page.

Then ask what you actually use it for. If the honest answer is which pages people read and where they came from, a full Google Analytics setup is overkill for that job, and you're paying for the overkill in page weight.

For that job, Plausible's script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, which helps keep your pages fast, and you don't need training to read the dashboard.

What's the heaviest third-party script you've found on your own site?

posts.title: Reel: your whole analytics script, 54 times smaller
posts.body:
Lightweight website analytics: Plausible's script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, and it sets no cookies.

Every visitor's browser downloads your analytics script on every page they open. If Google Analytics feels like overkill for what you actually track, that's a lot of code to ship for a few numbers. A smaller script means less to load, which helps your pages keep their speed.

Save this to check your own site: open your browser's developer tools, go to the Network tab, reload the page and look for the analytics request.

Plausible also collects no personal data, so your stats need no cookie banner. Plans and setup are at plausible.io, link in bio.

#GoogleAnalyticsAlternative #LightweightAnalytics #SiteSpeed #CookieFreeAnalytics

posts.videoScript:
Idea: a 54x smaller script means less for every visitor to load. Format: faceless screen recording with voiceover. Length: about half a minute. Search phrase: Google Analytics alternative. Save reason: the check-it-yourself step card near the end.

Beats:
Beat one, hook (first two seconds) | Visual: browser developer tools, Network tab filtered to 'plausible', one short request highlighted by the cursor | On-screen: Your analytics script, 54x smaller | Voiceover: "This one line is your whole analytics script."
Beat two, setup (a few seconds) | Visual: same Network tab on a second test page running Google Analytics, its tracking request highlighted | On-screen: Same check, Google Analytics script | Voiceover: "Plausible is a Google Analytics alternative, and its script is 54 times smaller."
Beat three, value | Visual: phone in hand scrolling a blog post on the Plausible test page | On-screen: Less code on every page view | Voiceover: "That's less code for every visitor to download, on every page they open."
Beat four, value | Visual: developer tools, cookie panel for the Plausible page, list empty | On-screen: No cookies. No personal data. | Voiceover: "It sets no cookies and collects no personal data."
Beat five, proof | Visual: slow scroll of Plausible's own stats dashboard | On-screen: So no cookie banner for your stats | Voiceover: "So your stats don't need a cookie banner."
Beat six, save card | Visual: cursor opening developer tools on any page, clicking Network, pressing reload | On-screen: Check yours: dev tools, Network tab, reload | Voiceover: "Check yours: open developer tools, go to the Network tab, reload."
Beat seven, call to action (final few seconds) | Visual: back to the single short request line, matching the opening shot so it loops | On-screen: Plans at plausible.io, link in bio | Voiceover: "Plans and setup are at the link in our bio."

Cover frame: the opening Network tab shot with 'Your analytics script, 54x smaller' in the upper middle, inside the grid's portrait crop.

Shot list (one desk session, under half an hour):
One. Screen recording on the team's own test page running only Plausible: open developer tools, Network tab, filter 'plausible', reload, hover the request. Record a couple of seconds before and after. Two takes.
Two. Screen recording on a second test page the team owns running only Google Analytics: same steps, highlight the tracking request. Before posting, check the sizes shown support the 54x claim; add no byte counts on screen.
Three. Phone held vertically, window light, lens wiped: scroll a blog post on the Plausible test page for a few seconds.
Four. Screen recording: the cookie panel on the Plausible test page, showing the empty list.
Five. Screen recording: slow scroll of Plausible's own stats dashboard. Turn on Do Not Disturb, close other tabs, hide the bookmarks bar.
Six. Screen recording: open developer tools on a neutral page, click Network, reload, for the save card.
Record the desktop full screen, then crop to vertical around the developer tools panel and zoom so request names are readable on a phone.

Sound: original voiceover recorded close to the mic in a quiet room. Optional quiet track from Instagram's commercially licensed library only, kept under the voice. Must work with no music.

Captions: burned in for every spoken word, centred in the middle third; keep all text and the highlighted request out of the bottom fifth of the frame and away from the right edge.

A's production detail is much stronger: shot list, cover-frame safe zones, faceless screen recording and burned-in captions. A non-expert owner could execute it.
A's carousel includes the honest 'not built for every job' slide, which fits the transparent brand voice.

B has a punchier, more scroll-stopping hook ('6 things your website doesn't need'). Its CTA is stronger, with the free trial and live demo as the main call to action. The trial and demo are mentioned in the insights, but they are not in the confirmed facts.

B is weaker on specifics. Its carousel body is thin, and it uses 8 hashtags with #GDPR, which edges toward compliance framing. It claims 'goals, funnels and revenue' on one page, which comes from the audience insight rather than a confirmed fact.

The trial offer is held back pending owner confirmation, which is cautious rather than a problem.

'Track goals, funnels and revenue' and 'key numbers on one page' are not among the confirmed facts.
The 'we earn money one way: people pay' claim goes slightly beyond the confirmed facts.

reasons: A uses only the confirmed facts. Where it wants a stronger offer (the free trial with no credit card), it flags that for the owner to check instead of asserting it. A's Reel is the smartest piece in either set. The 'check your own Network tab' step gives people a real reason to save the post, and the visual proof comes from the team's own test pages. The brief guards against unverified numbers on screen.

B's craft is punchier and more native to Instagram. The '6 things your website doesn't need' strikethrough carousel and the cookie-banner Reel hook would likely earn more engagement. Its trial CTA also fits the paid-customer goal better.

reasons: Both stay inside the confirmed facts and insights; neither invents customers, quotes or numbers, so the decision comes down to channel craft and usefulness.

B's hooks are Instagram-native and audience-relevant ('The first thing your visitors see might be a pop-up about your analytics', 'Who's behind your analytics, and how do they make money?'), with sound-off-friendly Reel structure, a clear cover frame, and the strongest available CTA (free trial, no card / live demo) that the insights identify as the main conversion lever.

A's visual briefs and NEEDS FACT flag are genuinely useful to a non-expert owner, and its caution about the trial is defensible; but B's briefs are also clear and buildable with far less reading.

B's carousel has a real execution flaw: it promises '6 things' in the title, hook and alt text but delivers only five 'need' slides, which the owner must fix before posting. That keeps the margin slight rather than clear.

emails.subject: What Plausible does (and what it doesn't)
emails.previewText: Clear numbers on one page. No cookies, no personal data.
emails.body:
Hi {{first_name|there}},

Thanks for signing up. Here's the short version of what Plausible is, so you can quickly decide whether it fits.

Plausible is website analytics built as a simple, privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics. Your traffic sits on one clear page. You won't need a training course or a tangle of menus just to see how your site is doing.

Here's what it doesn't do. It doesn't use cookies and it doesn't collect personal data. It builds no visitor profiles and runs no ad tracking. Plausible is an independent, EU-based company, and it doesn't sell customer data.

To be upfront, Plausible isn't right for every analytics use case. If you need deep custom reports on individual users, a heavier tool may suit you better. If you want straight answers about your traffic without the complexity, you're in the right place.

The fastest way to judge is to see it. The live demo lets you click around a working dashboard and decide for yourself whether it's the kind of simple you're after.

The Plausible team

emails.subject: Two things your analytics shouldn't cost you
emails.previewText: Page speed and a cookie banner.
emails.body:
Hi {{first_name|there}},

Most analytics setups quietly cost you two things.

1. Speed
Every script you add has to load. Plausible's script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, so measuring your traffic doesn't slow down the site you're measuring.

2. A cookie banner
Cookie-based analytics usually means asking visitors for consent. That's a banner people find annoying. It also leaves gaps in your numbers, because visitors who click 'reject' aren't counted. Plausible doesn't use cookies or collect personal data, so it doesn't need a cookie banner or a GDPR consent form.

One honest note: if other tools on your site set cookies, those tools may still need consent. Plausible removes analytics from that list.

If both of these matter to you, start a free trial and add the script to your site. You'll see your own traffic in Plausible soon after visitors start arriving, so you can compare it with what you use today.

The Plausible team

Hi {{first_name|there}},

Every analytics tool gets paid somehow. When it's free to you, it's worth asking what the business behind it gets in return.

Plausible's answer is short. The people who use it pay for it.

We're independent, self-funded and profitable. We have no investors pushing for growth at any cost. We're based in the EU, and we don't sell customer data. Our revenue comes from over 21,000 paying subscribers, and together their sites have sent more than 313 billion pageviews through Plausible.

That model is the reason the product stays the way it is. It's lightweight, it uses no cookies, it collects no personal data, and it puts clear numbers on one page. We have no reason to collect more about your visitors, because collecting it isn't how we make money.

If that's the kind of company you'd like counting your traffic, start a free trial. Add the script, watch your numbers for a while, and then decide whether to subscribe.

Thanks for reading,
The Plausible team

output.successMetric: Primary: share of sequence recipients who start a free trial within 30 days of email 1, and how many of those trials convert to paid. Per-email job metrics: email 1 is measured on demo-link clicks and replies. Email 2 is measured on comparison-page clicks. Email 3 is measured on trial starts from its link and replies to the P.S. Across all three, track unsubscribe and complaint rates. Ignore open rates, because Apple Mail Privacy Protection inflates them. Industry click-rate averages for automated flows are directional only and are not a target. The one test worth running: give email 3 a cookie-banner opening instead of the 'why pay' opening, and compare trial starts. Stop once each version has reached at least 1,000 recipients or after 4 weeks, whichever comes first. Keep the new version only if it is clearly ahead. On a small list, the cap is 200 trial signups per version.

reasons: A is much more operationally complete: double opt-in for the EU, exit on trial start, suppression rules, a sunset rule, authentication setup, a reply-to inbox and a branching path. A non-expert owner could use this as a real lifecycle flow.

A's copy sticks to confirmed facts and is honest about fit. It frames 'Google Analytics is free, why pay?' directly, offers a P.S. reply for fit checks, and cites the 30-day no-card trial, which is supported by the insights.
A's success metric is sharper: per-email job metrics, ignoring open rates because of Apple MPP, and a specific test with a stopping rule that matches the provided insights.
A flags the missing sender name with a NEEDS FACT marker instead of inventing one.

B's copy is good and readable, and its honest 'what it doesn't do' opener fits the brand voice. But it is thinner on lifecycle mechanics: no exit rule, no suppression logic, no branching, and no deliverability or compliance setup.

B makes some extra claims that are not in the confirmed facts: 'builds no visitor profiles and runs no ad tracking', 'no investors pushing for growth', 'visitors who click reject aren't counted', and 'you'll see your numbers soon'. These are plausible but unsupported.
B's metric choices are weaker: no test and no stopping rule, only 'use the first 30 days as the baseline'.
truthX: Says 'A person reads every reply' and promises 'we'll tell you straight whether Plausible fits', an operational promise not in the facts.
'Subscribers are the only people we answer to' is a mild embellishment.
truthY: 'Builds no visitor profiles and runs no ad tracking' goes beyond confirmed facts.
'No investors pushing for growth at any cost' is not confirmed; self-funded implies it but the phrasing is an embellishment.
Claims that cookie banners leave gaps in the numbers because rejecting visitors aren't counted is an unsourced assertion.
Says a heavier tool may suit users who need deep custom reports on individual users, a specific limitation not confirmed.

reasons: A is built as a working lifecycle flow, not just three emails. It has exit-on-trial, a branch that sends clickers straight to the trial ask, a reply pause, suppression and sunset rules, and a priority rule against the trial onboarding flow. B has none of this, so trial starters keep getting 'start your free trial' emails.

A gives each email a distinct job and its own metric: demo, then comparison page, then trial. That is a sensible progression. B asks for the trial in both email 2 and email 3 with nearly identical CTAs, which wastes a touch.

A's measurement is more honest and usable. It ignores open rates because of Apple Mail Privacy Protection and sets a single focused test with a stopping rule. B only says 'test subject lines' against a baseline.
A's email 3 tackles the real objection head-on ('Google Analytics is free, why pay?') and adds a strong reply-based P.S. that fits the transparent brand voice.
B's copy is honest and on-voice. It is especially good to note that other tools on the site may still need consent, which avoids overclaiming. Its strategic scaffolding is thin by comparison.
A's audience field is overloaded with deliverability setup and its test-cap wording is muddled, but this is operational noise, not a flaw in the strategy.
truthX: 'A person reads every reply' is an operational promise that has not been confirmed.
The '30-day free trial, no credit card required' detail comes from the site insights rather than the confirmed facts. The owner should verify it before sending.
truthY: 'No investors pushing for growth' is inferred from 'self-funded' rather than stated in the facts. It is minor.
'Builds no visitor profiles and runs no ad tracking' is an extrapolation beyond the confirmed facts. It is plausible but unconfirmed.

reasons: Both sequences stay inside the confirmed facts and use the four proof points correctly; neither invents customers, quotes or numbers, so this comes down to strategy and craft.

A's subject lines are sharper hooks for this audience: 'Google Analytics is free. Why pay for Plausible?' confronts the single biggest objection head-on in the inbox, and the P.S. reply hook ('tell us what you use GA for and we'll tell you straight if it fits') is a genuine conversion mechanic on-brand for a transparent, small-team company.

A includes operational logic a non-expert owner would otherwise miss: exit on trial start, branching clickers straight to the trial ask, pausing automation on reply, suppression/sunset rules, and a correctly reasoned decision to ignore open rates because of Apple Mail Privacy Protection. B's metric section is thinner and its 'test subject lines' instruction is generic.
A specifies one concrete A/B test with a hypothesis, stopping rule and sample cap; B sets no test design.

B has real strengths that keep the margin slight: the 'what it doesn't do' framing and the honest note that other cookie-setting tools may still need consent are excellent, on-voice touches, and its emails are slightly more conversational. But email 1 is long for a first touch, and emails 2 and 3 repeat the same CTA with less escalation.
A's audience field over-indexes on deliverability setup (SPF/DKIM/DMARC, postal address) which is useful but bloats a brief; it does not outweigh the better sequencing and measurement.
truthX: States 'Plausible is based in the EU, so use double opt-in' as if it were a requirement; double opt-in is best practice, not a confirmed legal necessity, and the fact only says the company is EU-based.

The 30-day free trial with no credit card and the live demo come from the research insights rather than the confirmed fact list; low risk since the brief's SWOT states them, but the owner should verify before sending.
truthY: 'Visitors who click reject aren't counted' and 'it leaves gaps in your numbers' are general industry claims about consent-gated analytics, not confirmed facts about Plausible or its rivals.
'Builds no visitor profiles and runs no ad tracking' and 'no investors pushing for growth at any cost' are reasonable extrapolations from facts 1 and 3 but go slightly beyond what is confirmed.

Email 1's 'If you need deep custom reports on individual users, a heavier tool may suit you better' is drawn from the SWOT weakness, not a confirmed product fact; the owner should check it matches the About page wording.

v0f.topIssue: The sequence stops after three emails and never uses its strongest friction-removers: the 30-day, no-credit-card trial and the GA4 import/migration path. That leaves the trial CTA weaker than it needs to be, with no follow-up for people who clicked but didn't start.

v22.topIssue: The sequence repeats Plausible's best-known claims (no cookies, 54x smaller, 21,000 subscribers) to people who already opted in to its blog or newsletter, likely already know them, and are not segmented by audience. It never uses fresher hooks such as AI-traffic visibility or agency and ecommerce use cases, so it adds little new reason to start a trial.

posts.firstComment: Plausible is independent, self-funded and profitable, based in the EU, and doesn't sell customer data. If you're weighing a switch away from Google Analytics, ask your question here and we'll answer it.

reasons: A's scripts are more production-ready: beat-by-beat visuals, on-screen text and voiceover, a shot list, a fallback if the owner has no consent tool, and sound and caption placement for each platform.
A keeps every claim tied to confirmed facts. It adds an honesty note to avoid implying full-site compliance, and it keeps 'GDPR compliant' off the screen.

A's hooks are built around a search phrase, 'analytics without cookies' and 'Google Analytics alternative', which suits discovery. The loop-back endings and the one-CTA discipline are good short-video craft.

B has a strong human angle: the talking-head cookie-banner hook, the on-camera caveat and the sugar-cube tabletop idea. It also includes the free-trial CTA, which fits the goal of getting paying customers.
B's script is simpler for a non-expert and its dev-tools first comment is a nice engagement hook, but its visuals are thinner and its on-camera setup is more demanding.

A's CTA only sends people to the live demo, with no trial mention, which is a weaker conversion push. B's trial CTA is a plus, but B's trial claim is not in the confirmed facts. It is supported only by the site summary in the insights, so it is probably fine.
truthX: The Instagram script says 'Link's in our bio' and the first comment says 'we'll answer it', which are small assumptions. 'One tiny script' is fine.
'Over 21,000 paying subscribers run it this way' is slightly loose, but the number is confirmed.
truthY: 'Most analytics tools set cookies and track personal data' is an unsupported generalisation, and 'Plenty of cookie banners exist mainly because of the analytics tool' is also unsupported.
'Free trial' and 'no signup needed to look around' are not in the confirmed facts. They come only from the insights text.
'So it won't drag your page speed down' and 'Faster pages' overstate what the 54x smaller script was confirmed to do.

The Instagram caption says 'That's the whole point of the sugar cubes', which is fine, but the cover labels the cubes 'Google Analytics' and 'Plausible' without the caveat about what the cubes represent.

reasons: A sticks closer to the confirmed facts. Its claims are scoped carefully: the banner point is limited to analytics, and the paperclips are flagged as illustrating a ratio, not a file-size measurement. It also bans 'GDPR compliant' and speed-score claims on screen.

A's production guidance is far more usable for a non-expert owner. It gives a beat-by-beat script with visuals, on-screen text and voiceover, a shot list, honest fallbacks if no consent tool exists, and safe-zone and caption guidance.

B's hooks are punchier and more native. 'This is your analytics script. And this is ours.' and the talking-head opener would likely stop more thumbs than A's clunky 'Analytics without cookies? Then your analytics needs no banner.'
B's free-trial CTA ties better to the paying-customer goal. A only pushes the demo, which is a soft action for a 90-day conversion goal.
B crams trust points, a caveat and proof into a few seconds, which dilutes focus. A keeps one message per video.
B's first comment (check cookies in dev tools) is a genuinely useful engagement play. A's first-comment caveat is also good and protects trust.
truthX: The voiceover 'you still see who came' loosely implies identifying visitors, which sits awkwardly with the no-personal-data claim.
truthY: 'Plenty of cookie banners exist mainly because of the analytics tool' and 'Most analytics tools set cookies and track personal data' are unsupported generalizations.
'So your pages stay fast' and 'won't drag your page speed down' overstate the confirmed claim that the small script helps maintain speed.
The cover line 'Same job. 54x lighter.' implies feature parity with Google Analytics, which isn't supported and conflicts with Plausible's own 'not for every use case' honesty.
The free-trial CTA relies on insight data rather than the confirmed facts. It is plausible, but the owner should verify it.

reasons: Both stick closely to the confirmed facts; neither invents numbers, customers or quotes, and both correctly use the live demo and trial CTAs from the insights.

B's hooks are stronger and more native to short video: 'That cookie banner on your site? It might be there just for your analytics' and 'This is your analytics script. And this is ours' open on pain or a visual reveal. A's TikTok hook ('Analytics without cookies? Then your analytics needs no banner') is keyword-stuffed and clunky as a spoken line.

B's scripts are tight, timestamped and shootable with a phone in an afternoon; the sugar-cube tower with labels is a clearer, more scroll-stopping 54:1 visual than a loose pile of paperclips. B also puts the honest caveat in the script itself rather than only in a comment.

A is extremely thorough (fallback plans, brand hex codes, caption safe zones, honesty notes) and arguably more rigorous, but much of that detail is overhead a small team doesn't need in a script deliverable and makes it harder to use. It does not reward length to say A's rigour is slightly better than B's on truth hygiene.
B carries a couple of mild unsupported generalisations about 'most analytics tools', which cost it a clear win, but they are not fabricated facts about Plausible.

# How to migrate from Matomo to Plausible

Matomo and Plausible both get you off Google Analytics, but they solve different problems. Matomo tries to do everything: dozens of reports, visitor logs, heatmaps, session recordings and a long list of settings. Plausible keeps the reports most site owners check every week on one page. It uses no cookies and collects no personal data.

If you've decided Matomo is more than you need, this guide shows you how to switch without losing your goals, your history or a week of data. Plan on about an hour of setup, then a few weeks of running both tools side by side.

## First: should you switch at all?

We'd rather you stay on Matomo than switch and regret it. Here is the honest trade-off.

**You keep:** visitors, visits, pageviews, bounce rate and visit duration. You also keep top pages, traffic sources, UTM campaigns, countries, devices, browsers and operating systems, plus goals, custom events, funnels and revenue tracking.

**You lose:** visitor-level reports, visitor profiles, heatmaps and session recordings. Plausible leaves these out on purpose because it measures traffic, not individuals.

**Stay on Matomo if** your team opens session replays or individual visitor logs every week and makes decisions from them.

**Switch if** most people on your team look at a handful of reports, you're tired of keeping Matomo's privacy settings up to date, or a consent banner is hiding visitors who click 'decline'.

Still unsure? Read [when Plausible is not the right choice](https://plausible.io/when-not-to-use-plausible) or open the [live demo](https://plausible.io/plausible.io), which shows Plausible's own website stats.

## Step 1: Audit what you actually use in Matomo

Before you touch any code, write down what Matomo does for you today. Most teams find they use a small part of it.

Go through your Matomo account and list:

- **Goals:** visits to a page (such as /thank-you), events, downloads, outbound clicks
- **Events:** your event categories, actions and names, and which ones anyone reports on
- **Ecommerce:** whether you track orders and revenue
- **Campaign links:** whether your links use UTM tags or Matomo's own campaign parameters
- **Custom dimensions:** extra data you attach to visits or actions, such as author, plan or logged-in state
- **Segments and scheduled reports:** who receives which email report
- **Settings:** timezone, excluded IPs and query parameters, and every site in a multi-site setup

Mark each item **must-keep**, **nice-to-have** or **unused**. Step 4 only covers the first two groups.

## Step 2: Start a trial and install the Plausible script

[Start a 30-day free trial](https://plausible.io/register). No credit card is required. Add your site and set the same timezone you use in Matomo so daily numbers line up.

Then install the script in whichever way suits your stack:

- **Any site:** paste the snippet into the head of every page, next to the Matomo tag. Do not replace it yet.
- **WordPress:** use the [official Plausible plugin](https://plausible.io/wordpress-analytics-plugin).
- **Google Tag Manager:** use the [Plausible GTM template](https://plausible.io/gtm-template).
- **JavaScript apps:** use the @plausible-analytics/tracker package on NPM.

The script is small. Plausible's tracking script is 2.5KB gzipped. Matomo's is 22KB, almost nine times larger. Compared with Google Analytics, Plausible's script is 54 times smaller. Once you remove Matomo in Step 7, your pages have less to load.

## Step 3: Run Matomo and Plausible side by side

Leave both tools running for most of your trial. This is the safest way to switch, and it shows you what changes.

**Your numbers will not match, and that is expected.** The biggest reason is consent. If Matomo uses cookies behind a consent banner, visitors who decline are not counted at all. Plausible uses no cookies, so it does not need an analytics consent banner and it counts those visitors. Many teams see more visitors in Plausible for this reason alone.

Other reasons for differences:

- Each tool defines a unique visitor differently. Plausible counts visitors without cookies.
- Bot filtering and excluded IPs differ.
- Timezones that don't match shift traffic between days.

What to compare instead of totals:

1. Do daily trends rise and fall on the same days?
2. Are your top 10 pages roughly the same, in roughly the same order?
3. Are your top traffic sources and campaigns the same?
4. Do goal conversions move together?

If all four line up, your setup is working.

## Step 4: Recreate goals, events and ecommerce tracking

Use your Step 1 list and this table to rebuild what you need.

| In Matomo | In Plausible |
|---|---|
| Visits, unique visitors, pageviews, bounce rate | Top graph on the main dashboard, compared with the previous period |
| Goal: visit a URL | Pageview goal |
| Events (category, action, name) | Custom event, with custom properties for the details |
| Custom dimensions | Custom properties |
| Ecommerce orders and revenue | Revenue goals, with a revenue breakdown in your reports |
| Funnels | Funnel analysis (Business plan) |
| Scroll tracking | Scroll goals |
| Segments | Filters and segments |
| Campaign tracking | UTM parameters, shown under Sources |
| Heatmaps, session recordings, visitor log | Not available by design |

A few tips:

- **Make goals specific with properties.** You can attach custom properties to pageview goals, custom events and scroll goals. For example, a broad Purchase goal can become a goal for one subscription plan or payment cycle. Funnel steps can use these more specific goals too.
- **Standardise campaign links.** Plausible reports campaigns from UTM tags. If your old links use Matomo-specific campaign parameters, switch your templates to utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign before you cut over.
- **Don't rebuild everything.** If an event was on your 'unused' list, leave it out. A short goal list is easier to read.

Check the [pricing page](https://plausible.io/#pricing) to see which plan includes the features on your must-keep list. Funnels are part of the Business plan.

## Step 5: Bring your historical data

You don't have to start from zero. Plausible's [CSV import](https://plausible.io/docs/csv-import) lets you bring historical stats into your dashboard. The import guide documents the file format Plausible expects. Export the Matomo reports you need, shape them to match that format, and import them.

Two more tips:

- **If you also ran Google Analytics,** you can [import Universal Analytics and GA4 data](https://plausible.io/docs/google-analytics-import) into the same Plausible dashboard. Plausible detects overlapping time ranges to avoid double counting.
- **Keep a Matomo archive.** Before you shut Matomo down, export the raw reports you might need later, such as yearly totals and ecommerce history, and store them somewhere your team can find them.

## Step 6: Reconnect your reports and your people

Analytics is only useful if the right people see it.

- **Search keywords:** connect [Google Search Console](https://plausible.io/google-search-console) to see the search terms that bring people to your site.
- **Existing dashboards:** if your team builds reports in Looker Studio, use the [Plausible connector](https://plausible.io/looker-studio-connector).
- **Clients and stakeholders:** share a dashboard publicly or privately with people who have never used analytics. Most can read it without training.
- **Agencies:** if you manage many client sites in Matomo, see how [Plausible works for agencies](https://plausible.io/for-freelancers-agencies).

## Step 7: Cut over and review your consent banner

When your side-by-side checks look right:

1. **Remove the Matomo tag** from every page, template, tag manager container and plugin. Use your browser's network tab to check that no Matomo requests are left.
2. **Update your privacy policy** to describe Plausible instead of Matomo.
3. **Review your consent banner.** Plausible doesn't use cookies or collect personal data, so it does not need an analytics cookie banner. Other tools may still need consent, such as ad pixels, chat widgets or embedded videos. Check what else sets cookies on your site, and ask your privacy advisor before removing the banner.
4. **Turn off Matomo,** or cancel your Matomo Cloud plan, once your archive is saved.

## If you self-host Matomo

Many Matomo users run it on their own servers. You have two options with Plausible:

- **Plausible Cloud:** managed for you, with no servers, updates or backups to maintain. Plausible is incorporated and hosted in the EU, and visitor data is processed only on European-owned infrastructure. See [EU hosting](https://plausible.io/eu-hosted-web-analytics).
- **Plausible Community Edition:** the [open source](https://plausible.io/open-source-website-analytics) version you run yourself. It leaves out some premium features, including marketing funnels, ecommerce revenue goals, SSO and the sites API. If you need those, choose Cloud.

## Frequently asked questions

**Will I lose my Matomo history?**
No, as long as you export it. Bring the stats you need into Plausible with CSV import, and keep a full Matomo export as an archive.

**Why does Plausible show more visitors than Matomo?**
The most common reason is the consent banner. Matomo does not count visitors who decline cookies, and Plausible doesn't need consent for analytics because it uses no cookies. Different definitions of unique visitors and different bot filtering also play a part.

**Do I still need a cookie banner after switching?**
Not for Plausible. Plausible uses no cookies and collects no personal data. You may still need a banner for other tools on your site, so review them before you remove it.

**How long should I run both tools?**
Run them together for most of your 30-day trial. A few weeks of overlap covers normal weekly patterns and gives you enough data to compare trends.

**Is Plausible right for agencies moving many client sites?**
Yes, if your clients want clear traffic and conversion numbers rather than visitor-level data. Start with one client site, check the side-by-side results, then roll it out to the rest.

## Try it alongside Matomo, with no commitment

Plausible is independent, self-funded and profitable, and it is paid for by its subscribers, not by selling data. More than 21,000 paying subscribers use it, and it has tracked over 313 billion pageviews.

The simplest way to decide is to see your own data. [Start your 30-day free trial](https://plausible.io/register) with no credit card, add the script next to Matomo, and compare the two before you commit. Want to look around first? [View the live demo](https://plausible.io/plausible.io).

# Can you replace Google Analytics and drop the cookie banner?

Yes, if your analytics is the reason you have a banner. Plausible Analytics counts visits without cookies and without collecting personal data, so it doesn't need a cookie banner or a GDPR consent form. You do give up some GA4 features: user-level reports, cohorts, retargeting audiences and multi-touch attribution. This page covers who should switch, who should stay, why your numbers will change and how to move without losing conversion tracking.

A note on who wrote this: we make Plausible, so we are one of the options here. We've tried to be plain about where it doesn't fit.

## What does "no cookie banner" actually mean?

It means your analytics stops being a reason to ask visitors for consent. Plausible doesn't set cookies or store persistent identifiers. To count unique visitors, it uses a random string that resets every day, so no one is followed from one day to the next or from site to site. Because no personal data is collected, there's nothing for a consent form to cover.

Check two things before you delete the banner:

- **Other tools on your site.** Ad pixels, chat widgets, embedded videos and some form tools set their own cookies. Removing GA4 removes the analytics reason for a banner, but those tools may still need one.
- **Your own legal sign-off.** We publish an independent legal assessment of how Plausible handles data. It's linked from our page on how Plausible counts visitors without cookies. Share it with whoever approves compliance for your site. This page describes what the product does; it isn't legal advice.

## Who should switch from GA4, and who shouldn't?

Switch if you mostly need visitors, sources, top pages and conversions on one screen. Stay with GA4 if your marketing depends on following individual users or building ad audiences from your analytics.

| You'll probably be happier with Plausible if… | You'll probably be happier staying on GA4 if… |
|---|---|
| You want analytics that doesn't need a consent banner | You build retargeting audiences from GA4 for Google Ads |
| You check a handful of numbers: visitors, sources, top pages, goal conversions | You report on cohorts and retention |
| Page speed matters and you want a light script | You need multi-touch attribution across many channels |
| You want an EU-based analytics provider that doesn't sell customer data | You need to see one visitor's path across sessions |
| You'd rather pay for analytics than have it funded some other way | You need a free tool and are fine keeping the banner |

If you tick boxes in both columns, run the two tools side by side for a couple of weeks and decide on your own numbers. The steps are below.

## What do you lose when you leave GA4?

Our own migration guide lists four GA4 features with no direct equivalent in Plausible:

1. **User-level reports.** Plausible shows totals and trends, not one visitor's history. That is the trade that makes counting without cookies possible.
2. **Cohorts and retention.** If you report on how many people from one month's signups came back the next month, Plausible won't build that report.
3. **Retargeting audiences.** You can't create ad audiences from Plausible data.
4. **Multi-touch attribution.** Plausible credits the last source before a conversion. If your reports split credit across several touchpoints, that model goes away.

Here's what you keep, all on one dashboard: traffic sources and UTM campaigns, goals and custom events, funnels, revenue on goals, and Google Search Console data.

## Why will your numbers look different after switching?

Expect Plausible and GA4 to disagree, mostly for reasons you can check:

- **Consent.** With a banner, GA4 can't count visitors who decline. Plausible doesn't need consent, so it counts them. This is our argument, so test it. Our cookie-banner traffic-loss calculator estimates the gap from your own consent rate, and running both tools side by side shows it directly.
- **Different definitions.** Plausible counts unique visitors per day with a rotating string, not with a long-lived cookie. GA4 "users" and Plausible "visitors" are not the same measure.
- **Ad blockers.** Some blockers stop analytics scripts, Plausible's included. migrateanalytics.com suggests serving the script through a first-party proxy to recover that traffic. Check our documentation for the current setup.
- **Setup gaps.** Single-page apps, subdomains and duplicate tags cause most of the surprises. There's a checklist in the next section.

## How do you switch without losing conversion tracking?

Map your GA4 conversions to Plausible goals before you remove anything, then run both tools in parallel. GA4 fires many events automatically. In Plausible, pageviews are tracked automatically and the actions you care about are goals you define. Most guides skip this mapping, so start with it.

| What you track in GA4 | How to track it in Plausible |
|---|---|
| page_view | Tracked automatically |
| Thank-you or confirmation page reached | Pageview goal on that URL |
| Purchase, sign-up or lead form submitted | Custom event goal |
| Purchase value | Revenue attached to the goal |
| Multi-step checkout or signup flow | Funnel built from your goals |
| UTM campaigns | Campaign and source reports |
| Search queries (via Search Console link) | Search Console integration |
| Remarketing audiences, user explorer | No equivalent |

Then work through these steps:

1. **List the GA4 events you actually report on.** Most sites have a few that matter, such as purchase, signup or lead, and many that nobody opens.
2. **Create a Plausible goal for each.** Use a pageview goal for "reached the thank-you page" and a custom event for a click or form submit.
3. **Add the Plausible script next to GA4.** Our migration guide notes that this has no meaningful impact on page speed. migrateanalytics.com suggests a 14-day parallel run, which covers two full weeks of normal traffic patterns.
4. **Check the four things that commonly break.** This list is adapted from migrateanalytics.com's cutover checklist:
   - A consent tool blocking the Plausible script. Plausible doesn't need consent, so exclude it from the tool.
   - Route changes in a single-page app not being counted as pageviews.
   - Goals counted twice because the script is installed twice.
   - Pageviews on subdomains missing.
5. **Import your GA4 history** so your trend lines carry on. Our step-by-step GA4 migration guide explains how and lists the current limits.
6. **Connect Google Search Console** to see the search queries that bring visitors.
7. **Remove GA4, then review your banner and cookie policy** against whatever else on the site still sets cookies.

## Does a lighter script make a difference?

Plausible's script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, so it adds very little to each page load. On a blog, a store or a landing page where speed counts, that means one less heavy file on every visit.

## Is Plausible free, and what are the other cookieless options?

No, Plausible is a paid tool, and you can try it free for 30 days with no credit card required. GA4 is still free and isn't going away, as Seline's roundup of Google Analytics alternatives notes. If cost decides it for you, the same roundup lists Umami, GoatCounter, Cloudflare Web Analytics and Microsoft Clarity as free options. Check how each one handles cookies and personal data before you assume it removes the banner, because "free" and "cookieless" are separate questions.

## Who runs Plausible?

Plausible is an independent, self-funded and profitable company based in the EU, and we don't sell customer data. More than 21,000 paying subscribers use it, and it has tracked over 313 billion pageviews.

## Questions people ask before switching

**Can I bring my Google Analytics data with me?**
Yes. Plausible can import your historical GA4 data, so your charts don't start from zero. Many alternatives can't import GA4 history directly, so ask about it whichever tool you choose. Our migration guide lists the current import limits.

**Is Plausible GDPR compliant?**
Plausible uses no cookies, stores no persistent identifiers and collects no personal data. We publish an independent legal assessment of that setup. Whether your whole site meets GDPR depends on everything else running on it, so your own legal sign-off should cover the full picture.

**Do I still need a cookie banner if I use Plausible?**
Not for Plausible. You may still need one for other tools that set cookies, such as ad pixels or embedded content.

**Do ad blockers affect Plausible?**
Some do. A first-party proxy can recover that traffic, and the parallel run will show how much your audience blocks.

**Does Plausible have funnels?**
Yes. You build funnels from the goals you set up, which is another reason to do the goal mapping first.

## Try it next to GA4

Start a 30-day free trial with no credit card required. Add the script beside GA4 and compare the two on your own traffic before you remove anything.

P.S. Want to see the dashboard before you install a script? The live demo shows a real Plausible site with real data.

Keep the keyword list tight and don't widen to broad match in month 1. On Meta, 5 USD/day is too little to test 4 concepts at once. Run 2 at a time (start with 'Remove the banner' and 'One page, no training'), then after about 3 weeks replace the weaker one with 'Size to scale' or 'AI traffic'. 90-day plan. Month 1: learn, and add negatives weekly. Month 2: move up to 50 USD from the weaker channel to the stronger one, based on cost per Free Trial Started. Month 3: keep the winners and test one new headline. Total spend never goes above 500 USD a month. Measure trials, then paying conversions after the 30-day trial. Most paying results from month 1 ads will only show up in month 2. Two brand checks before launch. First, your positioning stresses not selling data, and the insights say Plausible doesn't currently run paid ads. Decide whether running ads fits that stance, and measure with UTM tags plus your own Free Trial Started goal in Plausible instead of adding the Meta Pixel to plausible.io. Second, results are not guaranteed. Small budgets give noisy data, so judge after at least 4 weeks, not 4 days.

The next concept to swap in for a loser: speed for creators and publishers (54x smaller script), founder to camera. Provisional target, an assumption to replace with your real trial-to-paid rate and plan margin: $20 per trial start. The reasoning: if about one trial in four becomes a paying customer, that is about eighty dollars of ad spend per customer, roughly nine months of the entry plan at the third-party figure of $9 a month for 10k pageviews (vemetric.com, not confirmed on plausible.io, so the ads leave prices out). Test rule: judge on cost per trial start, then on cost per paying customer once trials have had time to convert, never on clicks or likes. After a Meta concept has spent twice the target (forty dollars), pause it if its cost per trial start is above $20 and swap in a new concept, not a reworded one. Google has only one ad group, so rather than pausing it early, review search terms twice a week for the first two weeks and then weekly, adding negatives each time; if after 4 weeks Google's cost per trial start is still above target while a Meta concept is below it, move Google's daily budget toward Meta within the same $500 cap, and the reverse if Google wins. Never add spend above the cap. Before approving, check that the free trial and the live demo are both live on plausible.io; the ads promise both but state no trial length or card terms. The brief's notes describe a 30-day trial with no credit card required; once you confirm that on the site, 'No Credit Card Needed' (22) can replace 'Plans for One Site or Many' as a headline and the Meta end frames can add the trial length. Copy says what the product does (no cookies, no personal data, no banner or consent form needed for Plausible) and does not promise legal compliance. Approve: budget split, bid strategy, conversion action, geography, AI Max and text-customization settings, final URL, Meta optimisation event, Advantage+ settings, the provisional $20 target, and each of the three concepts.

audiences.name: Site owners fed up with GA4

On the site, SEO consultant Cyrus Shepard calls Plausible a good fit for about 70% of websites struggling with GA4. Pitch them on 'one page, no training' and on the GA import, which keeps their history when they switch.

audiences.name: EU and privacy-regulated organisations (including public sector)
audiences.description: Teams that want to drop the cookie banner and keep visitor data on European-owned infrastructure. Plausible is built and hosted in the EU and collects no personal data. The site already has public-sector, compliance, DPA and procurement pages, which shortens a buying process that is usually slow. Lead with EU independence and data sovereignty.

audiences.name: SaaS companies and indie developers
audiences.description: Technical founders who care about script weight, open source and not lock-in. Hugging Face, Sentry, MongoDB and Basecamp are named users. This group is price-sensitive at higher traffic, compares against free self-hosted tools like Umami, and outgrows simple analytics once they need product analytics.

audiences.name: Agencies managing client sites
audiences.description: They need multiple sites, shared dashboards and a client-friendly UI. White-label is an existing offer. Growth covers 3 sites and Business covers 10. Fathom's entry plan covers 50 sites, so agencies will compare cost per site.

audiences.name: Ecommerce stores
audiences.description: Need revenue attribution and funnels without a consent banner hurting data quality. Those features sit in the Business plan. Speed-conscious merchants care about the script being 54 times smaller than GA.

audiences.name: Creators and publishers
audiences.description: Bloggers, newsletter writers and media sites that want simple traffic stats, scroll depth and AI-referral tracking. Traffic-based pricing becomes a sticking point as their pageviews grow.

competitors.name: Google Analytics 4
competitors.note: The default, and free in its standard version. It's the main thing Plausible replaces. Its weak spots: complexity, cookie and consent requirements, script weight, and sending data to a US ad company.

competitors.name: Fathom Analytics
competitors.note: The closest like-for-like rival: privacy-first, simple, cookieless. From $15/month for up to 100,000 pageviews and 50 sites, with a 7-day free trial. Stronger for agencies with many sites. Plausible's trial is longer (30 days vs 7).

competitors.name: Umami
competitors.note: MIT-licensed and free to self-host, with a free Cloud Hobby plan. Reviewers pitch it as the pick when the budget is $0. It competes for developers and side projects.

competitors.name: Simple Analytics
competitors.note: EU-based privacy-first rival with a conditional free cloud plan. It markets itself as the most privacy-maximal option and actively targets Matomo users with comparison content.

competitors.name: Matomo
competitors.note: The feature-heavy, privacy-capable GA replacement: free to self-host, cloud from about $23/month according to third-party reviews. It wins on depth and loses on simplicity. Plausible already has a comparison page.

competitors.name: Cloudflare Web Analytics
competitors.note: Free and bundled for Cloudflare users. Plausible already publishes a comparison page, which shows it's a real alternative in buyers' minds.

competitors.name: Seline
competitors.note: Newer cookieless tool that publishes 'best alternatives' lists ranking itself first and Plausible second. Its pitch is that funnels and revenue aren't locked behind a higher tier.

competitors.name: Rybbit
competitors.note: Newer entrant positioned on 'fair pricing that includes everything.' It's being promoted with articles that walk through leaving Plausible over price.

competitors.name: Open Analytics
competitors.note: Cookieless tool from $9/month that prices on events and pitches Stripe-linked revenue attribution as its edge over Plausible.

output.positioning: Plausible is the established, independent choice in privacy-first analytics. It has 21,000+ paying subscribers, 313 billion pageviews tracked, and named users like Stripe, Mozilla and Basecamp. It's EU-built, open source, and paid for by subscriptions rather than data. Rivals compete on one axis each: Fathom on sites per dollar, Umami and Matomo on free self-hosting, Seline, Rybbit and Open Analytics on including more features per tier. Plausible's defensible ground is trust. It's simple enough that clients understand it, light enough to protect Core Web Vitals, needs no cookie banner, and is run by a profitable EU company that isn't for sale. Over the next 90 days the sharpest message is GA4 replacement for people who never wanted to learn GA4, followed by EU data sovereignty. Lead with 'ditch GA4 and the cookie banner, keep your history.' Don't lead with features: newer tools are attacking on feature count, and Plausible shouldn't fight there.
output.pricingNotes: From the site: traffic-based plans, shown at 10k monthly pageviews as Starter $9/month (1 site, 3-year retention, goals, GA import), Growth $14/month (3 sites, 3 team members, shared links and dashboards), Business $19/month (10 sites, 5-year retention, funnels, ecommerce revenue attribution, Stats API). Enterprise is custom. Yearly billing gives 2 months free. 30-day free trial, no credit card. Observations: (1) The 30-day no-card trial is a real edge over Fathom's 7 days. Because the trial is that long, paid conversions from anything started in the next 90 days will show up with a lag of up to a month. (2) Third-party reviewers, not the official page, quote higher tiers, e.g. about $69/month at 1M pageviews. Treat that as unverified. Price at higher traffic is the most common complaint: an HN commenter called $500/year for 500k pageviews 'insane', while another replied that $42/month is a rounding error for a real business. That split tells you who to target: businesses, not hobbyists. (3) Funnels and revenue attribution are Business-only, and competitors (Seline, Rybbit) attack exactly that. It's also the most natural upgrade path. (4) Fathom's 50 sites from $15 looks better to agencies than Plausible's 3 or 10 sites, so agency messaging should lean on white-label and client-friendly UI rather than price per site. (5) No free tier is intentional and fits the 'pay with money, not data' story. Keep it, but frame the 30-day trial as the answer to 'is there a free plan?'

opportunities.title: Resolve the 'never spent a cent on advertising' claim before any ad goes live

Spending the $500/month makes that sentence false, which would hurt a brand built on transparency. Rewrite it honestly first (for example, explain that it grew without ads for years and is now testing a small search budget). Or decide to put the budget toward effort elsewhere. The owner should make this call.

opportunities.title: High-intent Google Search test on GA4 replacement searches
opportunities.why: Hypothesis: people searching to replace GA4 or remove cookie banners convert to trial at a useful rate when sent to the Migrate from GA4 page. Setup: $500/month, exact and phrase match only, on intent like 'GA4 alternative', 'Google Analytics alternative', 'cookieless analytics', 'analytics without cookie banner'. No competitor-brand bidding, which fits the voice. Primary metric: cost per trial start. Secondary: trial-to-paid at day 30-45. Stopping rule: review after the first $250 or 3 weeks. Pause any ad group with zero trials after 40+ clicks. End the test if blended cost per trial exceeds an agreed ceiling (owner to set based on lifetime value; assumption, no benchmark used). Paid results will lag up to a month because of the trial length.

opportunities.title: Trial activation email sequence
opportunities.why: With a 30-day no-card trial, the main lever for paid conversion is whether trial users install the script, import GA history and set a goal. opportunities.why: EU hosting on European-owned infrastructure, independence, a DPA and procurement pages are a differentiator US-hosted rivals can't match. Package it as a 'European analytics' landing page and outreach to EU agencies and public bodies.

opportunities.why: Seeing which AI tools (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude) send traffic and conversions is timely and gives GA4-frustrated owners a fresh reason to try Plausible now. It suits blog posts, social posts and a dedicated search ad group.
