findings.area: 1. Tracking and measurement · Blocker · Fix now (top 3)
findings.observation: Why top 3: none of the other fixes on this list can be verified without it. The primary CTA 'Start free trial' links to /register, but the page text does not show whether a goal fires on a completed signup or on the first payment (not verified). The About page says Plausible has 'never spent a cent on advertising', so there is probably no UTM convention or ad-conversion setup yet. Once $500/month goes to ads, you need trial signups and paid conversions reported by campaign. There is also a brand risk. Google Ads' standard conversion tag usually relies on cookies. Adding it to plausible.io would undercut your own line 'No need for cookie banners or GDPR consent' (to confirm with whoever handles your compliance).
findings.recommendation: (1) In Plausible, add a goal on completed registration, either a custom event on signup success or a pageview goal on the first page after signup. Add a revenue goal on the first paid subscription. (2) Use one UTM scheme for every ad, e.g. utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=no-cookie-banner. (3) Build a funnel: landing page → /register → signup complete → paid. (4) Measure ad results in Plausible by campaign instead of adding Google's conversion tag to your site. That means bidding on clicks, not conversions, at first. If you later want conversion-based bidding, treat it as a privacy decision first. (5) Baseline: from your own Plausible dashboard and billing records, pull the homepage visitor-to-trial rate and the trial-to-paid rate for the last 90 days. Write them down before changing anything. Effort: 2–4 hours. Impact (hypothesis): no direct lift, but it makes the ad spend and every later change measurable. Verify: a test signup with a test UTM shows up as a goal in Plausible, attributed to that campaign, the same day.

findings.area: 2. Trust conflict on the About page · Blocker for ads · Fix now (top 3)
findings.observation: Why top 3: this sentence becomes false on the day the ads start, and it contradicts the transparency the whole brand sells. The About page says: 'We have never spent a cent on advertising, affiliates or paid endorsements. Plausible grows because people recommend it...' A prospect who clicks an ad and then reads this sees the contradiction at the moment they are deciding whether to trust you.
findings.recommendation: Edit before launch. Suggested replacement: 'Most of our customers come to us because someone recommended Plausible. We have started running a small amount of advertising, paid for from subscription revenue like everything else. We don't pay affiliates or buy endorsements.' Keep the affiliates line only if it stays true. Effort: under 1 hour (about 15 minutes). Impact (hypothesis): protects trust with privacy-minded buyers who read About pages before paying. Verify: the page is updated, with the change dated, before the first ad goes live.

findings.area: 3. Paid traffic destination and message match · Blocker for ads · Fix now (top 3)
findings.observation: Why top 3: this is where the $500/month lands. The only candidate destination today is the homepage, and it is built for warm word-of-mouth visitors. It has a full mega-nav (Why Plausible, 7 'Who it's for' links, 4 Compare links, 5 Resources links) and two CTAs. The first content after the hero is an 8-item feature grid that opens with 'Automatic scroll depth tracking' and 'Monitor traffic from AI tools'. Proof, the founders' note and pricing all come after that. A cold, solution-aware searcher looking for cookieless or simpler analytics meets niche features before the reason they clicked. Ecommerce, SaaS, agency and public-sector buyers get nav links only.
findings.recommendation: Build one focused, noindexed landing page for a single ad theme: 'Google Analytics alternative, no cookie banner needed'. This budget supports one well-run theme better than several. Nav: logo, a Pricing anchor and Log in only. Sections: (1) a hero matched to the ad (see finding 4); (2) three core reasons: no cookie banner, one-page dashboard with no training, a script 54 times smaller than Google Analytics; (3) proof: 21k paying subscribers, the customer-name line, and the Rob Hope, Cyrus Shepard and John O'Nolan quotes; (4) a switching block with Google Analytics import and a link to the Migrate from GA4 guide; (5) pricing with the plan helper; (6) the objection FAQ from finding 6; (7) a repeat CTA. The H1 must repeat the ad headline's words. Check Google Ads trademark rules before using 'Google Analytics' in ad text; bidding on the keyword is a separate question. Build segment pages (SaaS, ecommerce, agencies) only once this page has data. Effort: 8–10 hours. Impact (hypothesis): a higher share of ad clickers start a trial because the first screen confirms why they clicked. Verify: trial signups per ad click, read as a 4–6 week directional trend.

findings.area: 4. Hero clarity, price signal and offer · Major · Fix now on the landing page, Test on the homepage
findings.observation: H1: 'Easy to use and privacy-friendly Google Analytics alternative'. Subhead: 'Plausible is powerful, lightweight analytics. No cookies, just insights. Made and hosted in the EU.' 5-second test: what = yes; who = partly (website owners are implied, never named); price or next step = partly (the trial is clear, the price is not); why this = partly. 'No cookie banner needed', a confirmed and concrete reason to switch, is missing from the hero, and 'powerful' is unsupported. Offer as it stands: a 30-day free trial with no credit card, plans from $9/month at 10k pageviews, and '2 months free' on yearly billing. Risk reversal: the no-card trial, Google Analytics import and open-source code. Urgency: there is no real deadline or capacity limit, so the page has no genuine urgency, and none should be manufactured. The yearly discount is a standing offer and should never be framed as time-limited.
findings.recommendation: Hero for the paid page and as a homepage test variant. H1: 'Simple Google Analytics alternative. No cookie banner needed.' Subhead: 'See your website's key stats on one page, without cookies or personal data. Our script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, and plans start at $9 a month.' CTA: 'Start my 30-day free trial'. Micro-copy: 'No credit card required. Import your Google Analytics stats.' Proof chip: 'Over 21,000 paying subscribers, including Stripe, Mozilla and Harvard University.' Before publishing, confirm that $9 is the monthly-billed Starter price at 10k pageviews, not the yearly-billing equivalent. Let the trial itself be the reason to act now; add no countdowns or 'limited time' labels. Effort: 1 hour. Impact (hypothesis): more visitors reach the trial because what, why and roughly how much are answered before they scroll. Verify: on the landing page, trial signups per ad click; on the homepage, the A/B spec in finding 10, using organic traffic.

findings.area: 5. Proof inventory and placement · Major · Fix now
findings.observation: Proof on the page, ranked by strength. Level 1, verifiable numbers: 21k paying subscribers, 313B tracked pageviews, 99.99% uptime over the last 90 days, and the script being 54 times smaller than Google Analytics ('135KB less JavaScript'). No method link was seen for the size comparison (not verified). Level 2, named quotes linked to their source posts: Clem Delangue, DHH, John O'Nolan, Cyrus Shepard, Rob Hope and Laura Roeder. Also named customer organisations: Stripe, Mozilla, MongoDB, Harvard University and Sentry. Level 3, demonstration: the live demo and the public, auditable source code. Level 4, risk reversal: the 30-day no-card trial, and open source so you're never locked in. Level 5, credentials: made and hosted in the EU; independent and profitable since 2018. Level 6, not proof: 'trusted by thousands of organizations', 'powerful', 'doesn't cut corners'. Placement problem: all Level 1 and 2 proof sits after the 8-item feature grid, and the hero has none. Rob Hope's 'Became a paying customer within 1hr of the 30-day trial' speaks directly to the trial decision but sits in the testimonial wall, far from any CTA.
findings.recommendation: (1) Add the proof chip under the hero CTA (finding 4). (2) Move the counters and customer-name line directly below the hero. (3) Link the 99.99% uptime figure to your Status page. Link the 54-times-smaller claim to its measurement if you have one published. (4) Replace 'trusted by thousands of organizations' with 'used by over 21,000 paying subscribers'. (5) Put the Rob Hope quote beside the pricing-section CTA. Put Cyrus Shepard's quote, which praises how easy the tool is for clients too, next to the one-page dashboard claim. Keep his 'not a ton of bells and whistles' line: the honesty helps. Effort: 1–2 hours. Impact (hypothesis): earlier, sourced proof reduces the 'is this a serious tool?' doubt among cold visitors before they reach the trial button. Verify: scroll depth to pricing and CTA clicks per visitor, before vs after (Plausible tracks scroll depth automatically).

findings.area: 6. Objection map · Major · Fix now
findings.observation: No voice-of-customer bank, review-site quotes or support data were available, so these objections come from the page copy, the testimonials and the business type, not from counts of real customer comments. Each entry gives the objection, where it comes up, and the answer from confirmed facts. (a) 'Do I still need a cookie banner?' Comes up in the hero. Answer: no cookies and no personal data, so no cookie banner or GDPR consent form is needed. Currently answered only mid-page. (b) 'Will I lose my Google Analytics history, and is switching a hassle?' Comes up next to the CTA and pricing. Answer: Google Analytics import, the Migrate from GA4 guide, and open source so you're never locked in. Currently one sentence mid-page ('You can even import your Google Analytics stats'); the guide is linked only from the nav and footer. (c) 'Will it slow my site?' Comes up in the hero and core reasons. Answer: the script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics. Answered mid-page. (d) 'Is it enough for what I track?' Comes up at the feature grid. Answer: goals, funnels, revenue tracking, AI-traffic and UTM campaigns, plus the honest 'when Plausible is not a fit' page. That page is linked from About but not from the homepage. (e) 'What will it cost at my traffic?' Comes up at pricing. See finding 7. (f) 'Can I trust a small company with my data, and will it last?' Comes up at the proof block and founders' note. Answer: independent, self-funded, profitable, EU-based, does not sell customer data, over 21,000 paying subscribers, running since 2018.
findings.recommendation: Place each answer where its objection comes up. Hero: (a) and (c), via finding 4. Directly above pricing, add a block headed 'Switching from Google Analytics?' with this body: 'Import your Google Analytics stats so your history comes with you. The code is open source, so you're never locked in.' End it with a link to the Migrate from GA4 guide. Below the feature grid, add a line: 'Not sure Plausible covers what you need? Read when Plausible is not a fit.' Linking to your own limits builds trust with buyers who are comparing tools. Next to the founders' note, put the independence facts as a short list rather than prose. Start collecting VoC now so the next round ranks objections by real counts. Sources: a one-question prompt when a trial ends without upgrading ('What stopped you from choosing a plan?'), your support and procurement inboxes, public reviews on G2 and Capterra, Hacker News and Reddit threads about leaving GA4, and, once ads run, the search terms report. Effort: 2–3 hours for the copy; VoC collection is ongoing. Impact (hypothesis): fewer Google Analytics users put off the trial over migration or data-loss worries. Verify: clicks on the migration link and the trial rate among visitors who view it (a Plausible funnel).

findings.area: 7. Pricing: choosing a plan · Major · Fix now
findings.observation: The slider defaults to 'Up to 10k monthly pageviews' ($9 / $14 / $19 a month). Plans are gated by features and number of sites. Nothing on the page tells a visitor which plan fits or how to find their own pageview count. Fathom's pricing page (https://usefathom.com/pricing) has a 'Not sure which plan you need?' box that suggests running Fathom alongside your current analytics during the trial. Fathom's trial is 7 days with a card required, so your 30-day, no-card trial is lighter friction. The pricing section doesn't use that advantage to answer the plan question.
findings.recommendation: Under the slider, add: 'Not sure how many pageviews you get? Start the 30-day free trial, add Plausible next to your current analytics, and see your real monthly pageviews before you choose a plan. No credit card required.' Under each plan name, add a one-line 'Fits you if' label in the buyer's terms. Starter: 'One site, just you.' Growth: 'Up to 3 sites and 3 team members, with shared and embedded dashboards.' Business: 'Up to 10 sites, plus funnels and ecommerce revenue attribution.' Enterprise: 'More than 10 sites, SSO or a managed proxy.' Effort: 2 hours. Impact (hypothesis): fewer visitors stall at the slider, because the trial becomes the way to answer the plan question. Verify: pricing-section CTA clicks, and the share of trials that pick a plan by day 30.

findings.area: 8. Prices may render only after JavaScript · Major · Fix now (to confirm)
findings.observation: From page source; not visually verified. The fetched text contains a script fragment, 'response.json()).then(data => currency=data.currency)', next to empty price slots ('/year /month') and '10k 10k'. This suggests currency, and possibly prices, are filled in client-side after a network request. Your audience likely runs privacy blockers more than average (assumption, based on the product's positioning). If that request is slow or blocked, a visitor or an AI browsing agent could see blank or shifting prices.
findings.recommendation: Server-render the USD prices for the 10k tier in the HTML as the default, then swap the currency after the lookup if it succeeds. Check the pricing section on a phone with JavaScript disabled and with uBlock Origin on. Effort: 2–4 developer hours. Impact (hypothesis): every visitor sees a price on first paint, and layout shift in the pricing block drops. Verify: the price appears in view-source and in the blocker test, and PageSpeed Insights reports CLS at 0.1 or below.

findings.area: 9. Signup form at /register · Not verified · Fix now (check)
findings.observation: Every trial starts at /register, but this audit did not open it. The field count, visible labels, password rules, email-verification step and any marketing-consent checkbox are all unknown. Cold ad visitors usually have less patience for a long form than referred ones (assumption). An unlabelled or long form would leak the conversions the rest of this list works to create.
findings.recommendation: Open /register on a phone and on a desktop and work through this list. (1) Count the fields. Keep only what is needed to create the account and add the first site; move anything else to onboarding. (2) Every field has a visible label, not placeholder-only text. This helps screen readers, password managers and AI browsing agents. (3) Repeat '30-day free trial · No credit card required' next to the submit button, and name the button after the outcome, e.g. 'Start my free trial'. (4) Any marketing consent is a separate, unticked box with plain wording and a privacy policy link. (5) Errors show inline. (6) The signup-complete goal from finding 1 fires here. Effort: 1 hour to check; fixes depend on what you find. Impact (hypothesis): removing even one unneeded field or confusing step raises the share of form starts that finish. Verify: the funnel step /register → signup complete in Plausible.

findings.area: 10. Section order: niche features before core reasons · Major · Test
findings.observation: The first content after the hero is an 8-feature grid: scroll depth, AI traffic, Search Console, UTM campaigns, real-time, codeless goals, funnels and bot filtering. The three reasons switchers usually give sit much lower, inside 'It's time to ditch Google Analytics': 'Simple analytics at a glance', 'Lightweight script' and 'No need for cookie banners or GDPR consent'. A skimmer meets advanced features before the reason to switch at all. Leading with depth does reassure power users, though, so the right order is uncertain. That makes this a test, not a fix.
findings.recommendation: Variant B: replace the first grid with three cards whose headings state the point. 'No cookie banner needed' (no cookies, no personal data, no cross-site tracking). 'All your stats on one page' (no training, no custom reports). 'A script 54 times smaller than Google Analytics' (135KB less JavaScript per visitor). Move the 8 features below them under 'Everything else you can track'. Write the test plan down before launch. Hypothesis: B raises homepage visitor-to-trial-signup. Audience: organic, direct and referral homepage visitors only; ad traffic goes to the landing page. Split: 50/50 by visitor, with a custom property 'variant' on the signup goal so Plausible reports each arm. Primary metric: visitor-to-trial-signup. Guardrails: pricing-section CTA clicks and day-30 trial-to-paid must not fall. Sample: before launch, calculate the per-arm sample size from your baseline rate (finding 1) and the smallest change you would act on, and record both. Run time: at least 2 full weeks to cover weekday cycles (assumption), and until the sample is reached. Decision rule: ship B only if it beats control on the primary metric at a two-sided 5% significance level with no guardrail drop. If the sample isn't reached in 6 weeks, keep control. No early stopping on a good-looking day. Effort: 2–3 hours to build, plus run time. Verify: the pre-written rule decides, not the dashboard mood.

findings.area: 11. Speed and mobile · Not verified · Fix now (check)
findings.observation: No PageSpeed, Core Web Vitals or screenshot data was provided. The page says the script 'won't affect your page speed or Core Web Vitals', so speed-conscious buyers will judge your own page by the same standard. The viewport tag, CTA position on a phone and tap-target sizes could not be checked from the text.
findings.recommendation: Run mobile PageSpeed Insights on https://plausible.io and on the new landing page. Check LCP at 2.5 s or under, INP inside Google's 'good' band, and CLS at 0.1 or under, Google's published thresholds. Watch for layout shift in the pricing slider (likely, to confirm). On a real phone, confirm that 'Start free trial' and the no-card line appear in the first screen, and that buttons and the slider handle are easy to hit with a thumb. Effort: 1 hour. Impact (hypothesis): poor scores would undercut your own speed claim; good scores become quotable proof. Verify: save the report and recheck after each layout change.

findings.area: 12. CTA wording and copy fog · Minor · Later
findings.observation: The primary CTA reads 'Start free trial' everywhere (nav, hero, each plan, footer), and the secondary is 'View live demo'. It is clear but generic; the trial length and no-card terms sit only in the micro-copy. Whether the two hero buttons carry equal visual weight could not be seen (not verified). Elsewhere, unsupported adjectives sit beside strong specifics: 'powerful, lightweight analytics', 'a simple, privacy-first alternative that doesn't cut corners', 'trusted by thousands of organizations'. The founders' block is long and 'we'-centred ('We invite you to take a look around... We'd be honored to have you as a customer'). That fits the brand voice but delays the visitor's own reasons.
findings.recommendation: Change the hero and footer buttons to 'Start my 30-day free trial', with 'No credit card required' directly under each. Keep 'View live demo' visibly lighter as the secondary option for buyers who want to see the dashboard first. Swap adjectives for facts already on the page. 'Powerful' becomes 'funnels, goals, revenue and AI-traffic tracking'. 'Thousands' becomes 'over 21,000 paying subscribers'. Trim the founders' note to its key lines (independent, self-funded, profitable, team of 10, running since 2018, funded by subscriptions, open source so you're never locked in) and keep it signed by Uku and Marko. Effort: 1–2 hours. Impact (hypothesis): small on the homepage, more useful on the paid page; faster scanning and more credible claims. Verify: CTA click rate and scroll depth past the founders' block.

quickWins: Before any ad runs, rewrite the About page line 'We have never spent a cent on advertising' so it stays true once the $500/month budget is live.
Add a proof chip under the hero CTA: 'Over 21,000 paying subscribers, including Stripe, Mozilla and Harvard University.'
Replace 'trusted by thousands of organizations' with 'used by over 21,000 paying subscribers'.
Add 'plans start at $9 a month' to the hero subhead, after confirming $9 is the monthly-billed Starter price.

Under the pricing slider, add: 'Not sure how many pageviews you get? Start the 30-day free trial, add Plausible next to your current analytics, and see your real numbers before you choose. No credit card required.'
Add a 'Fits you if' line under each plan name (Starter: 'One site, just you.').
Move Rob Hope's quote 'Became a paying customer within 1hr of the 30-day trial' next to the pricing CTA.
Add 'Import your Google Analytics stats' to the hero micro-copy, and link the Migrate from GA4 guide just above pricing.
Set up a signup-complete goal, a first-payment revenue goal and a fixed UTM scheme in Plausible, and pull your 90-day homepage baseline from your own dashboard before spending on ads.
Open /register on a phone and check field count, visible labels and an unticked, separate marketing-consent box.
output.clarityVerdict: Context: the page audited is https://plausible.io, a SaaS homepage that also carries the pricing section and is today the only destination for every visitor. Its single job is to get a 30-day free trial started. Current traffic is word of mouth and organic (per the About page). Planned traffic is cold search ads at $500/month from solution-aware buyers already looking for a Google Analytics alternative or cookieless analytics. Verdict: partly passes. The H1 'Easy to use and privacy-friendly Google Analytics alternative' says what this is (yes). Who it's for is implied, not stated (partly). The next step, a 30-day free trial with no credit card, is clear, but there is no price signal until the pricing section far down the page (partly). Why choose this is half there: privacy and 'made and hosted in the EU' appear, but 'no cookie banner needed' is missing from the hero, and 'powerful' is filler. Proof starts only after an 8-item feature grid. Warm visitors will cope; cold paid clicks have to scroll too far for the what, why and how much. Fix: put 'No cookie banner needed', the 54-times-smaller script, 'plans start at $9 a month' and the 21,000-subscriber proof chip in the first screen.
output.messageMatch: Not checkable yet: Plausible has never advertised, so there is no ad copy to compare with the H1. The page title, 'Simple, privacy-friendly Google Analytics alternative', matches the H1 well, which suits organic and comparison searchers. For the planned $500/month, don't send ads to the homepage. Pick one ad theme and send it to a focused, noindexed landing page whose H1 repeats the ad's words. Example pair: ad headline 'Analytics Without a Cookie Banner' → H1 'Simple Google Analytics alternative. No cookie banner needed.', with the same 30-day, no-card trial in both. At this budget, a landing-page A/B test is unlikely to reach a clear result (assumption; it depends on your cost per click). Test the angle in the ads instead (no cookie banner vs one-page dashboard vs 54-times-smaller script), measured by trial signups per campaign in Plausible, then carry the winner into the H1. Check Google Ads trademark rules before using 'Google Analytics' in ad text.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 1. Blocker · Now: Set up a signup-complete goal, a first-payment revenue goal, a landing → /register → signup → paid funnel and a fixed UTM scheme in Plausible. Measure ads by campaign there rather than adding Google's cookie-based conversion tag. Pull your 90-day baseline from your own dashboard first. Effort: 2–4 hours.
prioritizedFixes.why: Top 3 because no other change can be verified without it, and the ad budget would otherwise be spent blind. Keeping Google's tag off the site protects the 'no cookie banner' promise.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: No direct lift. It gives you a baseline and makes every later change measurable within the 90-day window.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 2. Blocker · Now: Rewrite the About page's 'never spent a cent on advertising' line before the first ad goes live. Effort: under 1 hour.
prioritizedFixes.why: Top 3 because the line becomes false the day ads start, and it contradicts the transparency the brand sells.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: protects trust with privacy-minded buyers who check the About page before paying.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 3. Blocker for ads · Now: Build one focused, noindexed landing page for the 'no cookie banner' angle, with minimal nav, a matched hero, proof directly under the hero, a switching block, pricing with a plan helper and the objection FAQ. Effort: 8–10 hours.
prioritizedFixes.why: Top 3 because this is where the ad money lands. The homepage shows niche features first and has a full mega-nav, which suits word-of-mouth visitors, not cold clicks.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: a higher share of ad clicks start a trial because the first screen confirms the ad's promise. Read as a 4–6 week directional trend.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 4. Major · Now on the landing page, Test on the homepage: Apply the hero rewrite (H1 'Simple Google Analytics alternative. No cookie banner needed.'; subhead with the 54-times-smaller script and 'plans start at $9 a month'; CTA 'Start my 30-day free trial'; proof chip with 21,000+ subscribers). Add no manufactured urgency. Effort: 1 hour.
prioritizedFixes.why: The current hero leaves out a concrete reason to switch, any price signal and any proof. No real deadline exists, so the trial itself is the call to act.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: more visitors start the trial without scrolling. Test on organic homepage traffic.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 5. Major · Now: Move the counters and customer-name line above the feature grid. Link the uptime figure to the Status page. Replace 'thousands' with '21,000 paying subscribers'. Put Rob Hope's trial quote beside the pricing CTA. Effort: 1–2 hours.
prioritizedFixes.why: Level 1 and 2 proof currently sits after 8 feature cards, and the quote about the trial decision is far from the trial button.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: more visitors scroll to pricing and click the CTA, measured with scroll depth and CTA clicks.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 6. Major · Now: Place each objection answer where it comes up (cookie banner and speed in the hero, a 'Switching from Google Analytics?' block above pricing, a 'when Plausible is not a fit' link below features, independence facts by the founders' note), and start collecting VoC. Effort: 2–3 hours, plus ongoing collection.
prioritizedFixes.why: Migration and data-loss worries get one buried sentence today, and no customer-language data exists yet to rank objections by real frequency.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: fewer Google Analytics users delay the trial; measure clicks on the migration link and trials among those who click.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 7. Major · Now: Add the 'Not sure how many pageviews you get?' helper under the slider and a one-line 'Fits you if' label under each plan. Effort: 2 hours.
prioritizedFixes.why: The slider defaults to 10k and plans are gated by features, with no guidance. Fathom's pricing page answers this question and Plausible's doesn't, despite having the lighter-friction trial.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: fewer visitors stall at plan choice, because the 30-day no-card trial becomes the way to decide.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 8. Major · Now (to confirm): Server-render the default USD prices so they show without JavaScript and survive privacy blockers. Effort: 2–4 developer hours.
prioritizedFixes.why: The page source suggests currency and prices load client-side after a fetch, which a privacy-heavy audience may block.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: every visitor and AI agent sees prices on first paint, with less layout shift in pricing.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 9. Not verified · Now (check): Audit /register on a phone for field count, visible labels, trial terms by the button, a separate unticked consent box, and the signup goal firing. Effort: 1 hour to check.
prioritizedFixes.why: Every trial passes through this form, and it was not observed in this audit.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Either confirms a clean form or finds a leak; measured by the /register → signup-complete funnel step.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 10. Major · Test: Run the pre-registered section-order test, with three core-reason cards before the 8-feature grid, on organic homepage traffic, a 50/50 split tagged by custom property, and decision rules written before launch. Effort: 2–3 hours to build.
prioritizedFixes.why: Leading with niche features may bury the reasons to switch, but it also reassures power users, so the answer is uncertain.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: better visitor-to-trial for basics-first visitors; ship only if the pre-set rule is met without a guardrail drop.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 11. Not verified · Now (check): Run mobile PageSpeed Insights on the homepage and the landing page, and check the hero CTA and touch targets on a real phone. Effort: 1 hour.
prioritizedFixes.why: Speed and mobile layout were not observed, and the product's own pitch is speed.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Either confirms a quotable strength or surfaces a fix, judged against Google's 'good' thresholds for LCP, INP and CLS.

prioritizedFixes.fix: 12. Minor · Later: Change the buttons to 'Start my 30-day free trial' and swap 'powerful' and 'thousands' for on-page facts. Trim the founders' note. Effort: 1–2 hours.
prioritizedFixes.why: The CTA is generic, and unsupported adjectives dilute specific, sourced claims.
prioritizedFixes.expectedEffect: Hypothesis: small gains in scanning and credibility, mainly on the paid page; measured by CTA click rate.

reasons: A is far more specific and actionable for the stated goal (paying customers from $500/month ads). It prioritizes measurement, the About-page contradiction, and a focused paid landing page, with effort, impact hypotheses and verification steps.
A catches the real risk that Google's conversion tag would undercut the no-cookie promise and gives a Plausible-native measurement and UTM scheme. B only briefly mentions checking cookies.
A gives a rigorous, pre-registered A/B test spec and is honest about what is unverified (/register, speed), and that a landing-page A/B test is underpowered at this budget.
A's hero rewrite and offer analysis are concrete and honest: it refuses manufactured urgency and flags confirming the $9 price basis before publishing.

B is solid and sensible; mapping ad groups to existing pages is a smart, cheap idea. But it is thinner, lacks a measurement foundation and baseline, and its trial-activation finding includes an odd '[NEEDS FACT]' leftover marker.
A is long and dense for a non-expert owner, which slightly hurts usability, and it relies on many page details beyond the confirmed facts. These appear to come from the site audit, not invention.
truthX: Cites named customers, quotes, 99.99% uptime, Fathom's 7-day card-required trial and plan details that are not in the confirmed facts. They are presented as observed from the site, and the 'confirm' caveats are only partial.
Suggests a proof chip naming Stripe, Mozilla and Harvard, which the insights say should wait until customer proof is confirmed.
truthY: Uses site-observed claims not in the confirmed facts: named customers and quotes, 99.99% uptime, the WordPress plugin/GTM/NPM package, and tier feature details.
Leaves a stray '[NEEDS FACT: ...]' marker in owner-facing text.
Says the About page line will be false once ads run, which is reasonable, but claims the pages /cookieless-web-analytics and /vs-matomo exist without verification.

reasons: A puts measurement first. It sets up a signup goal, a revenue goal, UTMs and a funnel, and records a baseline before the $500/month goes live. It also flags that Google's cookie-based conversion tag would undercut the 'no cookie banner' promise. B touches tracking only in passing and never builds the measurement base, so its ad and pricing fixes can't be verified.

A's hero rewrite is specific and ready to ship. It adds 'No cookie banner needed', the 54x-smaller script and a price signal. It also refuses manufactured urgency, which fits the brand. B keeps the H1 and offers only a subline tweak.

A's homepage test is properly pre-registered, with a hypothesis, guardrails, decision rule and no early stopping. It also warns that a landing-page A/B test is unrealistic at this budget and suggests testing angles in the ads instead. That is honest and evidence-based.
A covers the JS-rendered pricing risk and the unseen /register form, and labels both as unverified. Its labelling of assumptions and hypotheses is disciplined throughout.

B has one sharper strategic idea: route ad groups to existing intent pages (migrate, cookieless, vs-matomo, white-label) rather than building a new page. It also adds an Enterprise procurement path and activation emails, and it is tighter and easier for a non-expert to scan.
Both catch the About-page 'never spent a cent on advertising' conflict. Overall, A's depth, rigor and prioritization outweigh B's concision.
truthX: States Fathom's trial is 7 days with a card required, a competitor claim not in the confirmed facts and possibly outdated.
Proposes a hero proof chip naming Stripe, Mozilla and Harvard, although the insights say named customers need owner confirmation before use in marketing.
truthY: Clarity verdict claims visitors know 'who it's for' within five seconds, but the hero never names the audience.
Assumes dedicated pages such as /cookieless-web-analytics and /white-label-web-analytics exist and fit as ad destinations without stating that they were checked.
Asserts GA-history loss is 'the biggest switching fear' without customer data to support it.
